related_questions.question: What is the international treaty on asylum seekers?

text_blocks.snippet: The main international treaty concerning asylum seekers is the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol. This treaty defines who is considered a refugee and outlines their rights, as well as the obligations of states to protect them. The core principle of the convention is non-refoulement, meaning refugees should not be returned to a country where they face threats to their life or freedom.

list.title: 1951 Refugee Convention:
list.snippet: This treaty defines a refugee as someone who is outside their country of origin and is unable or unwilling to return due to a well-founded fear of persecution. It sets out the basic legal rights of refugees, such as the right to work, education, and freedom of movement, and it outlines the obligations of states to protect them.

list.title: 1967 Protocol:
list.snippet: This protocol removed the geographical and temporal limitations of the 1951 Convention, making its protections applicable worldwide and to those who became refugees after the initial cut-off date of January 1, 1951.

list.title: Non-refoulement:
list.snippet: This principle, central to both the Convention and customary international law, prohibits states from returning refugees to a country where they would face persecution.

list.title: Other relevant instruments:
list.snippet: Besides the Refugee Convention and Protocol, other international and regional instruments also address the rights of refugees and asylum seekers, including the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Article 14), the 1984 Convention Against Torture, and various regional refugee law instruments.

text_blocks.snippet: In essence, the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol are the cornerstone of international refugee protection, providing a framework for states to protect those fleeing persecution and violence.
